system_prompt: You are a security auditor assistant. Answer concisely, technically, and name the exact issue.

items.prompt: Threat model: users paste a URL; the backend fetches the page to render a link preview and shows the title to the user.
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: this is an ssrf (server-side request forgery) design risk — the attacker-chosen URL is fetched from your network position, reaching metadata endpoints, internal services, and localhost, with response content echoed back.
CONTROLS: https-only scheme, host allowlist, resolve and block private ranges after DNS, short timeout.
FIRST ACTION: put the allowlist + private-IP blocking in the design before implementation.

items.prompt: Design review: all services read one shared admin API key from a common config file. Threat-model verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: reject the shared key — it collapses blast radius to the whole system: one compromised service exposes admin capability over every service (a single finding covering the class).
ABUSE CASE: RCE on the weakest service yields the admin key and lateral access everywhere.
CONTROLS: per-service identities with scoped credentials (least privilege), secret-manager distribution.
FIRST ACTION: file as a design-gate blocker with a dated migration plan.

items.prompt: Threat model: the payment processor's webhook POSTs are processed as-is (no origin checks) and set order status from body fields.
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: tampering/spoofing critical — anyone who finds the URL can send a forged 'payment succeeded' event and get goods without paying (an unauthenticated write to your state machine).
CONTROLS: verify the processor's signature on every event, enforce a replay window (timestamp + event-id dedup), never trust status/amount fields outside the verified payload.
FIRST ACTION: reject unsigned events and ship signature verification.

items.prompt: Threat model: the SPA stores long-lived session tokens in localStorage.
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: move the token to an HttpOnly Secure cookie — localStorage is readable by any script on the origin, so one xss (or one compromised npm package) steals every visitor's session.
CONTROLS: HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie storage; SameSite blunts cross-site use.
RESIDUAL: csrf becomes the new concern — pair with SameSite=Lax and csrf tokens on state-changing routes.
FIRST ACTION: change token storage and add csrf protection in the same change set.

items.prompt: Threat model: a bulk CSV import endpoint accepts up to 10k rows and writes them into the shared orders table.
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: three abuse cases: authorization (bulk writes can cross tenant/ownership boundaries if the write layer doesn't scope rows — cross-tenant corruption), dos (a 10k-row unvalidated payload is unbounded memory/connection pressure — enforce a row cap), and tampering (partial commits corrupt data outside the validated path — make each import one atomic transaction, all-or-nothing).
FIRST ACTION: decide tenant scoping in the write layer at design time.

items.prompt: Architecture review: all services connect to the database with one shared superuser account for simplicity.
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: split into per-service scoped credentials (least privilege) — the shared superuser makes the blast radius the whole database: sql injection in any service reads and writes every service's data.
WHY: audit logs also lose attribution — actions can't be tied to a service.
MIGRATION: per-service users with schema-level grants, cut over one service at a time.
FIRST ACTION: scope the read paths first.

items.prompt: The auth dependency is flaky; the team proposes serving requests with auth bypassed during auth-service outages to protect availability.
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: fail closed for write/privileged routes — fail open turns every auth outage into an unauthenticated write window; availability is recoverable, data corruption is not.
DESIGN: cache validated sessions with a short ttl so brief outages are invisible; queue writes with explicit 'unavailable' responses.
FIRST ACTION: make deny-by-default explicit in the middleware.

items.prompt: Multi-tenant design: every table has tenant_id and every query filters it manually. Architecture-level concern?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: the manual filter is the defect — one forgotten WHERE clause is a cross-tenant leak (idor class), and convention cannot be grepped into safety.
CONTROLS: enforce scoping in the data layer (orm/repository default scope requiring tenant context — an invariant, not a habit), plus a regression test class that fails on cross-tenant reads.
FIRST ACTION: make a query without tenant context raise an error.

items.prompt: Architecture: secrets are injected into workloads via env vars written in k8s manifests checked into git.
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: reject for real credentials — the manifest is a secret in source (committed to git/repo): any reader, fork, or CI log extracts it, and env vars are readable via /proc and dashboards.
CONTROLS: secret manager / operator mounting secrets as files at boot, rbac-limited; only non-sensitive config stays in git.
FIRST ACTION: rotate everything already committed, then move to mounted secrets.

items.prompt: The design embeds a third-party analytics SDK on every page, sending email and address with each event.
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: gate the flow — data minimization first (opaque user id, no pii), because the data permanently leaves your control to a third party whose SDK also ships third-party code into your origin (supply-chain xss surface).
CONTROLS: documented purpose/retention/deletion path with the vendor, SDK only on pages that need it.
FIRST ACTION: require the vendor deletion API in the design or drop the pii fields.

items.prompt: A diff replaces password hashing hashlib.md5(pw) with hashlib.sha256(pw). Review verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: request changes — this is a lateral move between still-weak choices: sha256 is an unsalted fast hash, as GPU-crackable as md5 for passwords.
FIX: a password kdf — bcrypt or argon2 — with a migration path (verify the old hash at login, rehash with the new scheme).
NOTE: approving it would falsely signal the class is fixed.

items.prompt: A PR adds dependency `python-dotenvy` (small new package, 40 stars). Review comment?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: request changes — suspected typosquat: the official package is python-dotenv; near-miss names are the classic squat pattern, and tiny low-star packages are cheap to publish maliciously.
FIX: verify the name letter-by-letter on the registry, install the official package, and if the squat was ever installed: purge the lockfile entry and rotate the credentials CI exposed.
FIRST ACTION: registry check before any install.

items.prompt: A refactor removes @login_required from a view and instead checks auth inside one nested branch 'for performance'. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: request changes — relocating a guaranteed wrapper check into a conditional branch invites the bug where a new branch or early return skips authorization entirely; authz changes must strengthen, never relocate.
FIX: keep the middleware/decorator (it is one cheap session lookup), measure first, and if hot, cache session validation.
NOTE: performance fixes belong in caching, not in weakening the gate.

items.prompt: A PR adds GET /api/debug/dump-users returning all users' emails, 'temporary support tooling'. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: block — missing access control plus pii over-fetch: unauthenticated debug routes historically persist beyond their expiry and dump pii to anyone who finds them.
IF GENUINELY NEEDED: behind admin role, audit-logged, rate-limited, field-minimal — or build it on the existing admin UI.
FIRST ACTION: remove the route from the PR; fix the route-template access-control gap it reveals.

items.prompt: A diff adds `EXPORT_WEBHOOK_SECRET = 'whsec_abc123'` used to sign outbound events. Review comment?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: request changes — hardcoded secret in source: anyone with repo read access can forge outbound event signatures, and rotation currently requires a deploy.
FIX: read from the environment/secret manager; and because it entered git history: rotate the secret now — file removal is not rotation.
FIRST ACTION: rotate, then inject via env, then add a secret-scanning gate.

items.prompt: API audit: GET /api/invoices/{id} is behind authentication middleware. What is the next mandatory check?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: object-level authorization (bola/idor) — the middleware proves the caller is a user, not that this invoice belongs to them.
CHECK: the query must be scoped to the caller (owner/tenant context in the WHERE clause), not just fetch by id.
VERIFY WITH: a test requesting another user's id and asserting 404 — run it against every id-parameterized route.

items.prompt: API audit: POST /api/users does User(**request.json) where the payload may include is_admin and plan. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: reject — mass assignment: the client sets privilege fields (is_admin, plan) directly, escalating from a public route.
FIX: an explicit allowlist schema ({name, email, password}), unknown fields rejected; role/plan decided server-side only.
VERIFY WITH: a test posting is_admin=true asserting rejection.
FIRST ACTION: fix signup first — it is reachable by anonymous callers.

items.prompt: API audit: error responses include full stack traces to help client developers debug. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: remove — stack traces in responses are information disclosure: paths, library versions, and internal structure map the attack surface for attackers.
FIX: a generic error envelope (code + correlation id) to clients; full detail stays in structured server-side logs keyed by that id.
FIRST ACTION: replace the global exception handler.

items.prompt: API audit: a public search endpoint runs user-supplied regex patterns over large documents. Required controls?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: three controls: rate limit (regex over large inputs is cpu-bound — a redos/dos amplifier), input bounds (cap pattern length and complexity; reject nested quantifiers), and a bounded execution timeout so pathological patterns degrade instead of pinning workers.
WHY: unbounded public CPU work is a denial-of-service path even with perfect auth.
FIRST ACTION: rate limit + length cap.

items.prompt: API audit: the third-party webhook handler processes body.status directly with no sender verification. What must be added?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: signature verification + replay protection before trusting the body — an unverified webhook is an unauthenticated write to your state machine (forged 'payment succeeded' is the canonical abuse).
CONTROLS: verify the sender's signature per event, timestamp window + event-id dedup for replay, idempotent processing.
FIRST ACTION: reject unsigned events (log them), implement verification via the vendor SDK.

items.prompt: CI audit: a workflow uses pull_request_target, checks out the PR head, and runs tests with repo secrets in scope. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: restructure now — critical: pull_request_target runs privileged on untrusted code; a malicious PR edits the test script itself and exfiltrates every secret in scope.
FIX: split the trust — pull_request (unprivileged, no secrets) runs the untrusted code; privileged steps run only on protected refs after review.
FIRST ACTION: strip secrets from that job today.

items.prompt: CI audit: a workflow step contains `run: echo Deploying ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}`. Any issue?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: yes — command injection: the PR title is attacker-controlled text interpolated into a shell command on the runner (a crafted title executes arbitrary commands).
FIX: pass it through env: (TITLE: ${{ ... }}) and quote "$TITLE" — env intermediaries never execute.
SWEEP: grep all workflows for ${{ inside run: with user-influenced events; the pattern repeats.

items.prompt: CI audit: the deploy job uses a long-lived cloud access key stored as a repo secret. Better design?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: oidc federation — the pipeline exchanges short-lived tokens for cloud credentials: no static key to leak, scope bound to the deployment.
IF UNAVAILABLE: least-privilege per-environment keys with rotation; never one prod key shared across jobs.
WHY: a static key is one leak away from full prod access with no expiry.
FIRST ACTION: enable oidc for the CI provider; migrate one environment at a time.

items.prompt: CI audit: PR builds run on a self-hosted runner whose containers mount /var/run/docker.sock. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: remove it — docker.sock is root on the host: untrusted PR code escapes the container and owns the runner machine, then the internal network.
FIX: ephemeral per-job vm runners for untrusted builds; no sock mounts anywhere; self-hosted runners reserved for protected-ref deploys.
FIRST ACTION: move PR builds off the self-hosted pool today.

items.prompt: What supply-chain gates should the pipeline run before deploy, and why?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: four failing gates: dependency audit (pip-audit --strict / npm audit) on the lockfile, image scan (trivy) on the built image, sbom emission (so the next Log4Shell-class event is answered in hours), and artifact signing with signature verification at deploy (unverifiable artifacts don't ship).
WHY: each gate turns a class of surprise into a deterministic build failure.
FIRST ACTION: add the dependency audit gate.

items.prompt: Container review: Dockerfile uses FROM node:latest, installs, and runs node server.js as root. Give the hardening diff.
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: four changes: pin the base image (version tag or digest — latest is mutable and non-reproducible), USER node (never root), copy package manifests and npm ci --omit=dev (reproducible install), and a .dockerignore excluding .env/.git so secrets never enter image layers.
RESIDUAL: readOnlyRootFilesystem at runtime with a tmpfs for /tmp.
FIRST ACTION: pin + USER — two lines.

items.prompt: Container review: a Deployment sets privileged: true 'to install tools at boot'. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: reject — privileged grants near-host power (devices, namespaces, kernel interfaces); installing tools is a build-time job, not a runtime excuse.
FIX: bake the tools into the image; set privileged:false, allowPrivilegeEscalation:false, capabilities drop ALL.
IF A DEVICE IS NEEDED: pass that specific device only.
FIRST ACTION: rebuild the image with the tools; strip the privilege block.

items.prompt: Container review: app pods run with the default service account, which is bound to cluster-admin. Risk and fix?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: critical — a compromised pod inherits cluster-admin, so one web-rce becomes instant cluster compromise.
FIX: per-app service accounts with least-privilege rbac scoped to their own namespace; automountServiceAccountToken:false where the app never calls the k8s api; cluster-admin reserved for break-glass humans.
FIRST ACTION: strip cluster-admin from app pods and fix rbac per app.

items.prompt: Container review: no workload sets resource requests or limits. Why is this a security finding and what do you set?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: limits are the blast-radius control for runtime defects: one memory-leaking pod can oom every neighbor on the node.
SET: requests+limits on every container (memory limit ≈ 2× observed steady-state rss), plus liveness probes so leaky pods recycle instead of accumulating.
FIRST ACTION: measure current usage for a week, then roll out limits namespace by namespace.

items.prompt: Container review: the namespace has no network policies; any pod can reach any pod. Hardening plan?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: default-deny then allowlist: deny all ingress and egress in the namespace, then add explicit allows per dependency (app→db, app→cache); separate public-facing pods into their own namespace.
WHY: east-west freedom is how a web-rce becomes internal-network compromise; policies close that path regardless of app bugs.
FIRST ACTION: apply default-deny in staging — the breakage list is your dependency map.

items.prompt: Secrets response: an AWS access key was found committed in git history, last modified 2022. What is the response sequence?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: treat as compromised: revoke/deactivate the key first (history keeps it live — deleting the file changes nothing), then review cloud logs for its use since 2022, then rotate to a scoped replacement; history rewriting is optional hygiene, not a fix.
WHY: scanners harvest repos continuously; an old live key is almost certainly replayed.
FIRST ACTION: deactivate the key before any investigation.

items.prompt: Secrets review: every service reads the same master API token for the payment vendor. What do you require instead?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: per-service vendor credentials — scoping is the least-privilege boundary you control: one compromised service must not carry the payment capability of all services.
REQUIRE: vendor sub-keys per service (or oidc federation if offered), per-service revocation paths, and a rotation runbook naming owners and triggers.
INTERIM: proxy vendor calls through one internal service so only it holds the master key.

items.prompt: Secrets review: the plan is to rotate all secrets manually every quarter. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: automate or it won't happen — manual rotation silently stops after the first busy quarter, and unrotated credentials accumulate forever.
REQUIRE: dual credential rotation (the overlap pattern: issue new, switch consumers, revoke old) so rotation is zero downtime and boring; start with the highest-value classes (cloud keys, db passwords, signing keys).
FIRST ACTION: automate one class end-to-end, then copy the pattern.

items.prompt: Secrets response: an engineer pasted a production database password into a PR comment yesterday. Response?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: rotate-and-revoke immediately — the credential left the vault (PR comments sync to tools and are org-readable), so it is compromised regardless of the comment being deleted.
THEN: rotate via the dual-credential path, check db logs for unexpected clients since the paste, and fix the workflow that let a human hold prod secrets (break-glass with approval + audit).
FIRST ACTION: rotate now.

items.prompt: Secrets review: staging and prod auth services share the same JWT signing key 'for parity'. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: split the keys — a token minted in staging (weak configs, test accounts, looser logging) must not verify in prod; shared keys turn a staging compromise into a prod authentication bypass.
REQUIRE: distinct keys per environment and the environment embedded in the token audience so cross-env replay fails structurally.
FIRST ACTION: issue a prod-only key and enforce the audience check.

items.prompt: IR: at 3am a service account performs 50k unusual S3 reads. What are the first 30 minutes?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: assume active exfiltration until proven otherwise — (1) revoke/quarantine the credential to stop the bleed, (2) export the relevant logs to append-only storage, (3) scope it: buckets, data class, source ips, since when, (4) open the incident record with a timeline, lead, and scribe.
DO NOT wait for more certainty while access is live.
FIRST ACTION: revoke the key — containment outranks analysis.

items.prompt: IR: ops wants to rebuild a compromised server from scratch immediately. Response as security lead?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: snapshot first, rebuild after — forensics on the live host (persistence mechanisms, tooling, timeline) is what separates eradication from recurrence; rebuilding destroys the evidence while the attacker's forgotten backdoor (new ssh key, cron job, api token) survives elsewhere.
SEQUENCE: snapshot disk+memory → export logs → rebuild from known-good → rotate what the host held → monitor the rebuilt path.
FIRST ACTION: start the snapshot.

items.prompt: IR: a stolen API key was used for two hours last night. What belongs in the impact statement?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: scope by the credential's permissions, verified by its access log: the use window, what the key could reach (worst case), what the logs show it actually touched (actual case), and the data classes involved.
OUTPUT: two lists — definitely accessed and possible-but-unconfirmed — with log evidence; never claim 'no data accessed' before the log analysis supports it.
FIRST ACTION: export the key's full api log for the window.

items.prompt: IR: ransomware is actively encrypting a file share. Immediate sequence?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: isolate, don't power off: network-isolate affected hosts (memory evidence survives), sever the share, revoke implicated credentials, engage leadership/legal/insurance (clocks start now), and restore only from offline-verified backups after the entry path is closed — restoring earlier re-encrypts the restore.
DO NOT: reboot affected hosts or pay.
FIRST ACTION: isolate the share and hosts while the triage call convenes.

items.prompt: IR learning: the entry point was an unpatched library CVE. What does a good postmortem produce?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: five assignable actions with owners and dates, at least one converted into an automated gate: patch + pin the library; a ci dependency-audit gate failing on known cves (the compounding fix); inventory coverage review (why the sbom/scan missed it); detection review (why we learned from impact, not logs); playbook update.
FORMAT: blameless, timeline-anchored; 'be more careful' appears nowhere.
FIRST ACTION: ship the ci gate.

items.prompt: Logging review: the app logs to stdout only and ops greps files on hosts. Security verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: ship to a central append-only store outside the app's write path — host-local logs are invisible across services and attacker-writable (a compromised app edits its own trail).
REQUIRE: structured json events with stable fields (utc timestamp, actor/principal, action, resource, result, source ip, request id), defined retention, and app credentials that cannot delete security logs.
FIRST ACTION: add the shipper plus the backbone event types.

items.prompt: Logging review: which events must be logged for incident response to function?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: the backbone set — login success/failure, permission denied, password/mfa/role changes, data export/download, secret/vault access, config changes, token issuance/revocation, admin actions — because every investigation walks exactly these events.
FIELD RULE: every event carries the authenticated principal, never just an ip (identity-bound attribution is what makes 'who did what' answerable).
FIRST ACTION: audit which of these the system emits today; the missing ones are the finding.

items.prompt: Logging review: dashboards show cpu and error rates. Which security detections are missing?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: four rule classes on the backbone events: credential attack (login failure bursts per account and per source — stuffing), privilege movement (role/admin changes, permission-denied spikes from bola probing), exfiltration shape (export volume anomalies per principal), and control-plane changes (config/secret/token events outside change windows).
START COARSE with owners; silence hides intrusions.
FIRST ACTION: the failure-burst rule — cheapest, highest hit rate.

items.prompt: Logging review: the team proposes logging full request bodies 'for debugging'. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: not at full fidelity — bodies carry passwords, tokens, and pii, which turns the log store into a second credential database with weaker access control (the secrets_in_logs class at system level).
FIX: field-level redaction middleware on the logging path (structural, not per-developer diligence), plus sampling limited to specific endpoints behind a documented flag.
FIRST ACTION: the redaction middleware — it protects every current and future endpoint.

items.prompt: Logging review: audit logs are stored as a table in the same database the application writes to. Verdict?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: move them — the audit log's threat model must assume the app is hostile: an attacker with app-level db access (sql injection, compromised credential) edits or deletes the trail precisely while they are active.
REQUIRE: an external append-only store with separate credentials (no update/delete grants for the app), retention lock, and ship-as-written streaming rather than idle-time batches that lose the last window of an attack.
FIRST ACTION: duplicate the stream to the external store now.

items.prompt: Restraint check: GET /health returns {status:'ok', version:'1.4.2'} with no authentication. Finding?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: no finding — an unauthenticated health endpoint returning status and a version string is standard practice; it grants no capability and discloses nothing sensitive.
NOTE only: dropping the version string is a judgment call if your threat model treats version-targeted exploits as a concern — not a defect.
VERDICT: approve as-is.

items.prompt: Restraint check: a diff renames a variable from `temp` to `temporary_path` and adds type hints. Any security comment?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: no security concern — the diff changes naming and typing only: no new sinks, no boundary movement, no credential or authorization change.
VERDICT: approve on security grounds; style is a separate review track.
NOTE: do not manufacture findings on harmless diffs — reviewer credibility is what makes real blocks land.

items.prompt: Restraint check: a test fixture contains the string API key 'sk-test-0000000000000000' clearly marked as dummy. Finding?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: no finding — clearly-marked dummy credentials in test fixtures are standard and harmless; scanners will hit them but the pattern is explicitly non-live.
VERIFY only: it is not a real environment credential dressed as a dummy, and real credentials never live in fixtures.
VERDICT: approve.

items.prompt: Restraint check: a feature renders static marketing content from a CDN — no user input, no accounts, no stored data. Full threat model needed?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: no meaningful threat surface — there are no input paths, no identity, no data assets, no attacker-reachable state: nothing to model beyond content integrity, which the cdn's tls covers.
VERDICT: skip the full model; do not manufacture stride coverage for a surface with nothing to attack.

items.prompt: Restraint check: a single external IP port-scans you at a steady 20 connections/day for weeks. Incident?
items.reference:
RECOMMENDATION: not an incident — steady low-volume scanning is internet background noise; what matters is that the exposed surface is minimized and patched, which is standing work.
ACTION: confirm the scanned ports are intended-public, keep the trend in a dashboard, and page only on change-from-baseline (volume spikes, new sources, internal-range targeting).
VERDICT: no page, no incident record.
